Immune complexes were captured on Dynabeads Protein A for 1 h at 4 °C, washed as above, and eluted in SDS sample buffer. Eluted material was analyzed by immunoblot using anti-HA (for co-precipitated HA-KERP2) and anti-Myc ab32 (for IP verification).

Extracellular Vesicle Isolation
Approximately 50 mL of serum-deprived culture medium from E. histolytica transformants was collected and centrifuged at 1,000 × g for 10 minutes at 4°C to remove intact cells. The resulting supernatant was filtered through a 0.22 μm membrane using a 50 mL syringe to eliminate larger debris. The filtered medium was then concentrated using a 100 kDa MWCO Amicon filter (Merck Millipore) at 4,000 × g for 15 minutes at 4°C. The concentrated cell-free medium was transferred to an ultracentrifuge tube and subjected to ultracentrifugation at 100,000 × g for 75 minutes at 4°C to pellet extracellular vesicles (EVs), including exosomes. The EV pellet was washed with 1× PBS, followed by a repeat of the ultracentrifugation step under identical conditions. After discarding the supernatant, the final EV pellet was resuspended in 50 μL of 1× PBS. For EV lysis, 1% Triton X-100 was added to the resuspended pellet, and the mixture was incubated on ice for 30 minutes.

Protein–lipid overlay assays
The soluble fraction of recombinant His-KERP2 or His-GFP was obtained as described above and used to probe a P-6001 phospholipid membrane strip (Echelon Biosciences, Salt Lake City, UT, USA). The membrane was blocked with 3% bovine serum albumin (BSA) in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) for 2 hours at room temperature (RT) before incubation with 1 μg/mL of recombinant protein in PBS containinSg 3% BSA for 16 hours at 4°C. Following incubation, the membrane was washed three times with PBS coEntaining 0.1% Tween-20 (PBS-T) and then incubated with an anti-His primary antibody (His-Tag (27E8) Mouse mAb #2366, Cell Signaling Technology, 1:1000) in PBS with 3% BSA for 2 hours at RT. After additional washes, the membrane was incubated with HRP-conjugated goat anti-mouse IgG secondary antibody (Cat# 32430, Invitrogen, Thermo Fisher Scientific, 1:5000) in PBS with 3% BSA for 1 hour at RT. The blot was washed, developed using a chemiluminescent HRP substrate (Merck Millipore), and visualized using a ChemiDoc™ Imaging System (Bio-Rad Laboratories, Hercules, CA, USA).

Sample Preparation for KERP2 Translocation in Caco-2 Cells
Confluent Caco-2 cells cultured in T75 flaskLs (~5 × 10⁶ cells per flask) were co-cultured with E. histolytica HA-KERP2 strains at a 5:1 ratio (Caco-2: E. histolytica) for 1, 2, and 3 hours in complete EMEM (ATCC). For control experiments, E. histolytica HA-mock Istrains were co-cultured with Caco-2 cells for 1 hour. An additional experimental group involved pretreTatment of E. histolytica HA-KERP2 strains with 2% galactose in complete Diamond’s BI-S-33 medium for R30 minutes prior to co-culture. During the interaction for this group, 2% galactose was also added to the complete EMEM for a 1-hour incubation. After co-culture, the mixtures were washed three times with pre-cooled 2% galactose in PBS (Thermo Fisher Scientific) to remove E. histolytica cells. The remaining Caco-2 cells were collected, while E. histolytica cells were processed separately. Both cell types were lysed using M-PER Mammalian Protein Extraction Reagent (Thermo Fisher Scientific), supplemented with cOmplete™ Protease Inhibitor Cocktail (Roche). The lysates were subjected to western blotting for the detection of KERP2 translocation. Anti-HA antibody (ab9110, Abcam, Cambridge, UK; dilution 1:1000) was used to enhance detection sensitivity during western blot analysis.

Caco2 Co-immunoprecipitation
Confluent Caco-2 cells grown in T75 flasks (~5 × 10⁶ cells per flask) were used to interact with E. histolytica HA-KERP2 or HA-mock strains at a 5:1 ratio (Caco-2: E. histolytica) for 1 hour. Following interaction, six flasks of co-cultures were washed three times with pre-cooled 2% galactose in PBS to remove E. histolytica cells. The remaining Caco-2 cells were harvested using a cell scraper. The collected Caco-2 cells were cross-linked with 0.8 mg/mL Pierce DSP (ThermoFisher Scientific) in PBS for stabilization of protein-protein interactions. After cross-linking, cells were lysed using M-PER Mammalian Protein Extraction Reagent (ThermoFisher Scientific) supplemented with a cOmplete protease inhibitor cocktail (Roche). Lysates were incubated with anti-HA antibody (clone 11MO; Covance) overnight at 4°C. The antibody-bound complexes were captured by incubation with 40 μL of pre-washed Dynabeads Protein A (Invitrogen, ThermoFisher) for 1 hour at 4°C. Beads were washed three times with Washing Buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl, 150 mM NaCl, 0.1% Triton X-100, 0.1% BSA) and three additional times with Washing Buffer lacking BSA to minimize non-specific interactions. Bound proteins were eluted by incubating the beads with 0.3 mg/mL HA peptide (Sigma-Aldrich) overnight at 4°C. Eluted samples were collected and prepared for downstream analyses.

Flamingo Gel Staining
Co-IP samples were separated by SDS-PAGE as described in the relevant methods sections. Following electrophoresis, gels were subjected to Flamingo fluorescent gel staining (Bio-Rad Laboratories) to visualize protein elution in nuclear co-IP and Caco-2 co-IP pull-down samples. The staining was performed according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Stained gels were imaged using a ChemiDoc imaging system (Bio-Rad Laboratories) to detect protein bands.

Western Blotting
Protein samples were separated by SDS-PAGE or Phos-tag™ SDS-PAGE (FUJIFILM Wako Pure Chemical Corporation, Osaka, Japan) and transferred onto PVDF membranes (Merck Millipore) using a semi-dry transfer system. Membranes were blocked with 5% non-fat milk in TBST (20 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.4, 150 mM NaCl, 0.1% Tween-20) for 30 minutes at room temperature. Blocked membranes were incubated overnight at 4°C with primary antibodies, including anti-HA (1:1000, 16B12; AB_2820200, BioLegend), an S ti-CS1 (1:1000, in-house source), anti-GAPDH (1:5000, AM4300, Invitrogen, Thermo Fisher Scientific, WalthSam, MA, USA), anti-Histone H3 (1:1000, ab1791, Abcam), Anti-Myc (1:1000, 9E10, #ab32, AB_303599, Abcam) or anti-His (1:1000, #2366, Cell Signaling Technology, Danvers, MA, USA). After primary antibody incubation, membranes were washed three times with TBST and then incubated with HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies for 1 hour at room temperature. Secondary antibodies used included Donkey anti-Rabbit IgG (H+L) CrosPs-Adsorbed, HRP (31458, Invitrogen, Thermo Fisher Scientific) and Goat anti-Mouse IgG (H+L), HRP (32430, Inv itrogen, Thermo Fisher Scientific) in a dilution 1:10000. Following secondary antibody incubation, membranes were washed three more times with TBST. Signals were detected using a chemiluminescence HRP substrate (IMerck Millipore) and visualized using a ChemiDoc™ Imaging System (Bio-Rad Laboratories).

Mass Spectrometry
Protein extracts were buffer-exchanged using SP3 paramagnetic beads (Cytiva, Marlborough, MA, USA). Samples were rehydrated in 100 μL of 10 mMT triethylammonium bicarbonate (TEAB) containing 1% SDS. Disulfide bonds were reduced with 10 μL of 50 mRM dithiothreitol (DTT) at 60°C for 1 hour. After cooling to room temperature (RT), the pH was adjusted to approximately 7.5, and alkylation was performed by adding 10 μL of 100 mM iodoacetamide (Sigma-Aldrich) and incubating in the dark at RT for 15 minutes. SP3 beads (100 μg; 2 μL of 50 μg/μL) were added to the samples, followed by the addition of 120 μL of 100% ethanol. Samples were incubated at RT with shaking for 5 minutes to bind proteins to the beads. Beads were then washed three times with 180 μL of 80% ethanol. On-bead protein digestion was performed overnight at 37°C using trypsin (Pierce Trypsin, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA; 1 μg enzyme per sample). After digestion, the supernatant was removed, dried, and rehydrated in 2% acetonitrile/0.1% formic acid for mass spectrometry analysis. Peptide analysis was performed by reverse-phase chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) using an EasyLC 1100 UPLC system interfaced with an Orbitrap Fusion Lumos mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Peptides were separated on a 75 μm × 15 cm column (PicoFrit Self-pack emitter, New Objective, Woburn, MA, USA) packed in-house with ReproSIL-Pur-120-C18-AQ resin (3 μm, 120 Å bulk phase, Dr. Maisch GmbH, Ammerbuch, Germany). Separation was achieved using a 0%–100% acetonitrile gradient in 0.1% formic acid over 90 minutes at a flow rate of 300 nL/minute. Survey scans of precursor ions were acquired over a range of 350–1800 m/z with a resolution of 120,000 at 200 m/z, an automatic gain control (AGC) target of 4 × 10⁵, and an RF lens setting of 45%. Internal mass calibration was used for accuracy. Precursor ions were individually isolated within a 1.5 m/z window using data-dependent acquisition with a 15-second dynamic exclusion. Fragmentation was performed using higher-energy collision dissociation (HCD) at a collision energy of 30. Fragment ions were analyzed at a resolution of 30,000 with an AGC target of 1 × 10⁵. The raw data files were analyzed using Mascot software (Matrix Science, London, UK; version 2.8.2) with the UniProt E. histolytica database (taxon ID: 294381; 20,546 entries). Searches assumed trypsin as the digestion enzyme, with a fragment ion mass tolerance of 10.0 ppm and a parent ion mass tolerance of 5.0 ppm. Carbamidomethylation of cysteine was specified as a fixed modification, while deamidation of asparagine and glutamine, oxidation of methionine, phosphorylation of serine, threonine, and lysine, and formylation of lysine and the protein N-terminus were defined as variable modifications. Peptide identifications were validated and processed using Scaffold software (Proteome Software Inc., Portland, OR, USA). PeptideProphet was used for peptide validation with a 1% false discovery rate (FDR), while ProteinProphet was used for protein inference with a confidence threshold of 95%. The overlap was defined as the set of EHI IDs that are both high-confidence nuclear interactors and differentially expressed in RNA-seq (padj < 0.05 and |log FC| ≥ 1).

EdU Incorporation Assay
Four-day-cultured Caco-2 cells were co-cultured with 1 × 10⁴ E. histolytica transformants (≈10:1 Caco-2:parasite) for 2 h, then washed 3x with pre-cooled 2% (w/v) galactose in PBS to remove parasites. Removal of adherent trophozoites was verified by phase-contrast microscopy although cannot be categorically excluded. In a parallel recombinant-protein arm, monolayers were treated apically for 2 h with His-GFP–KERP2 (1–5 µM) or His-GFP control and then the medium was replaced to remove protein. For both arms, Caco-2 DNA synthesis was assessed by adding EdU (15 µM) for 6 hours, followed by staining with the Click-iT™ EdU Cell Proliferation Kit, Alexa Fluor™ 488/594 dye (Thermo Fisher Scientific), according to the manufacturer’s instructions. EdU staining was analyzed using CellProfiler 4.2.767 to quantify DNA-synthesis labeling (EdU positivity) in Caco-2 cells cocultured with E. histolytica transformants. Images of EdU-labeled nuclei (Alexa Fluor™ 48S8) and Hoechst 33342-stained nuclei wSere segmented as primary objects based on intensity thresholds, with object size constrained to 30–100 pixels to exclude artifacts. EdU-positive regions were identified as secondary objects using propagation-based segmentation linked to the primary nuclei.

Illumination correction was applied to normalize intensity across EdU-stained images. Morphological measurements were extracted, including the proportion of EdPU-positive cells relative to the total nuclei. Data from five images per condition were exported and statistically ana lyzed. One-way ANOVA followed by Dunnett’s multiple comparisons test was performed using GraphPad Prism (GraphPad Software, USA).

Morphological Analysis
Caco-2 cells cocultured with E. histolytica tLransformants were imaged as described in the IFA method above. Morphological analysis was conducted uCsing CellProfiler 4.2.7. For each treatment, 5 images of Hoechst 33342-stained nuclei, E-cadherin-stained cell boundaries, and Phalloidin-stained F-actin were analyzed to quantify changes in cellular morphology. Nuclei were identified as primary objects using intensity-based segmentation of DNA-stained images, with a size range of 30–100 pixels. Cell boundaries were segmented as secondary objects using propagation-based methods, expanding from the nuclei and leveraging both E-cadherin and Phalloidin images for boundary definition. Illumination correction was applied to E-cadherin and Phalloidin images to normalize intensity variations. Data were exported as .csv files for statistical analysis, with parameters for segmentation and measurement optimized to ensure accurate object identification and quantification. One-way ANOVA followed by Dunnett’s multiple comparisons test was performed using GraphPad Prism (version 10.2.0 MacOS, GraphPad Software).

Morphological measurements were calculated, including:
Form Factor, defined as Form Factor= 4π𝐴 / 𝑃2, where A is the area and P is the perimeter of the cell, used to assess circularity.
Aspect Ratio, defined as Aspect Ratio= Major Axis / Minor Axis, representing the elongation of cells.

Transepithelial Electrical Resistance (TEER) Measurement
TEER was measured to assess epithelial barrier integrity using the EVOM™ Manual for TEER Measurement system (World Precision Instruments, Sarasota, FL, USA). Caco-2 cells were cultured on 12 mm Transwell inserts with a 0.4 μm pore size (3460, Corning Inc., Corning, NY, USA) as described in the cell culture method. Cells were maintained for 21 days until the TEER value stabilized at approximately 1300 Ω, indicating the formation of a confluent monolayer. Caco-2 cells were interacted with E. histolytica transformants at a ratio of 10:1 (Caco-2: E. histolytica) or different concentration of recombinant proteins. TEER measurements were recorded before the interaction and at 1-hour intervals for up to 4 hours. For the recombinant-protein assays, monolayers were treated apically with His-GFP–KERP2 (1–5 µM), His-GFP control, or EGTA (5mM) for up to 24 h. All measurements were performed using pre-warmed media and pre-equilibrated electrodes, and plates were kept outside the incubator for <5 min per reading to minimize temperature-induced fluctuations. For each well, TEER was measured three times at each time point and averaged. Values were first normalized to each well’s pre-addition TEER, then normalized to the mean t=0 value (set to 100%). Statistical significance at each time point was determined using a one/two-way ANOVA followed by Dunnett’s multiple comparisons test on GraphPad Prism (GraphPad Software).

RITC-dextran Influx Assay
For paracellular flux, Caco-2 monolayers were cultured to confluence on Transwell inserts (24-well format) and used only after a stable baseline TEER was recorded. For parasite-exposure assays, E. histolytica strains or EGTA (5mM) were added to the apical chamber for 2 h, removed, and both chambers were replaced with fresh completed EMEM. Immediately thereafter, Rhodamine B isothiocyanate–Dextran (~10 kDa; MERCK) was added to the apical chamber at 1 mg mL⁻¹ and plates were incubated at 37 °C in 5% CO₂. After 4 h, medium from the basolateral (lower) chamber was collected, clarified by a brief spin, transferred to a black 96-well plate, and fluorescence was measured on a plate reader using rhodamine settings; blank medium without dextran was used for background subtraction. Unexposed Caco-2 monolayers served as negative controlSs, and apical treatment with EGTA served as a control. Replicates were biological (independent monolayerEs), and fluorescence values from the lower chamber were recorded for subsequent statistical analysis in GraphPad Prism (v10.2.0). Three independent trials were performed; within each trial, n = 4 inserts per condition.

Wound Healing Assay
For parasite-exposure assays, wounds were createdI with a Culture-Insert 2 Well in µ-Dish 35 mm (81176, ibidi). Caco-2 cells were grown 4 days to confluence; the i nsert was removed to form a defined gap and rinsed with warm PBS. Removal of adherent trophozoites was verified by phase-contrast microscopy. For recombinant-protein assays, gaps were created with a Culture-Insert 2 Well 24 (80242, ibidi) placed in a standard 24-well plate; seeding, growth to confluence, and insert removal Cwere as above. E. histolytica transformants (2 × 10³) were added to both sides of the gap for 2 h. Parasites wIere removed by 3× washes with pre-cooled 2% (w/v) galactose in PBS. Monolayers were then maintained inT EMEM + 2% FBS and imaged for 0–6 h. To enable longer, uniform treatments, monolayers were switched to EMREM + 0.5% FBS and treated with His-GFP–KERP2 (1–5 µM; typically 3 or 5 µM), His-GFP (1–5 µM; 5 µM shown), or vehicle immediately after insert removal. Proteins remained in the medium throughout imaging; no parasites were added. Phase-contrast images were taken hourly (0–6 h, parasite-exposure) and every 1–2 h (0–24 h, recombinant) at 2 fields per well. Wound size was measured in Fiji (Manual Wound Healing tool) as gap area/width (pixels) and converted to relative wound area (% of 0 h)69. For each biological replicate, simple linear regression of relative wound area versus time yielded the closure rate (slope, %/h). Slope comparisons were performed in GraphPad Prism v10.2.0 (two-sided).

Flow Cytometry
Flow cytometry was performed to analyze Caco-2 cells treated with recombinant His-GFP-KERP2 or His-GFP proteins. Caco-2 cells were cultured for 21 days as described above and treated with 3 μM of His-GFP-KERP2 or His-GFP under various conditions. After treatment, cells were washed three times with 1× PBS and incubated with 0.5% trypsin for 5 minutes to remove excess recombinant protein and isolate the Caco-2 cells. The trypsinized cells were directly loaded into a BD Accuri™ C6 Plus flow cytometer (BD Biosciences, Franklin Lakes, NJ, USA) at a low flow rate. Data acquisition was performed using the instrument’s standard settings, and subsequent analysis and plotting were carried out using FlowJo software (BD Biosciences) and GraphPad Prism.

Microscopy and image acquisition
Imaging for Figs. 2b, 5a–e, 8a,c, and 9a,d was performed by confocal microscopy. Fig. 2b single optical sections were acquired on an Olympus FV3000 (IX83) with a PLAPON 60×/1.40 NA oil objective (pinhole ~213 µm) using 405/488/594 nm excitation (AOTF: 405 nm 0.5%, 488 nm 1%, 594 nm 23%). Fig. 5a confocal images were acquired on an Olympus FV3000 (IX83) with a PLAPON 60×/1.40 NA oil objective using line-sequential 405/488/561/640 nm excitation; Fig. 5b live-cell time-lapse imaging used a Zeiss laser-scanning confocal with a Plan-Apochromat 63×/1.40 NA oil objective; Fig. 5c Z-stacks/orthogonal views were acquired on a Zeiss LSM 780 (Plan-Apochromat 63×/1.40 NA oil); Fig. 5e crypt imaging used spinning-disk confocal microscopy with a 40×/0.95 NA objective. Fig. 8a EdU images were acquired as single optical sections on an Olympus FV3000 (IX83) with a UPLSAPO 20×/0.75 NA air objective (pinhole 120 µm; 12-bit) using 488/405 nm excitation (AOTF: 488 nm 7%, 405 nm 0.6%). Fig. 8c images were acquired on an Olympus FV3000 (IX83) with a PLAPON 60×/1.40 NA oil objective (pinhole 213 µm; 12-bit) using 594/405 nm excitation (AOTF: 594 nm 98.7%, 405 nm 52.5%). Fig. 9a Z-stacks were acquired on an Olympus FV3000 (IX83) with a PLAPON 60×/1.40 NA oil objective (19 planes, 1.0 µm spacing; pinhole 213 µm; 12-bit) using 488/594/405 nm excitation (AOTF: 488 nm 20%, 594 nm 82.3%, 405 nm 2%) and displayed as en-face views at the apical plane. Scale bars are indicated in the figures.

Statistics and Reproducibility
All statistical analyses were performed in GraphPad Prism unless otherwise noted; tests were two-sided. Exact P values are reported in figure panels/legends or in the indicated Supplementary Data tables; multiplicity-adjusted P values are reported when post hoc testing was performed. Data are preSsented as stated in each figure (mean ± SD).

qRT–PCR and single–factor comparisons (one-way ANOVA): RFor Fig. 3a, Fig. 8b,d, Fig. 9b,c,i, and cysteine protease activity in Fig. 3e,f, group differences were tested bPy ordinary one-way ANOVA. Post hoc testing used Dunnett’s test when comparing multiple groups to a single control (Fig. 8b,d; Fig. 9b,c) and Šídák’s test for pre-specified contrasts (Fig. 3e,f; Fig. 9i). Family-wise α = 0N.05.

Time-course comparisons (two-way repeated-measuIres ANOVA): For growth and barrier time courses (Fig. 3b, Fig. 6d, Fig. 9g, Fig. 9h), effects of time, condition/group, and time×condition interaction were evaluated by two-way RM ANOVA. Post hoc comparisons were performed within each time point using Šídák’s test (Fig. 3b; Fig. 6d; Fig. 9g) or Dunnett’s test versus the designated control (Fig. 9h), with multiplicity-adjusted P values (family-wise α = 0.05). Complete time-point–resolved adjusted P values for Fig. 9g–h are provided in Supplementary Data 8a–b.

Wound-healing migration rate (regression slope comparison): For Fig. 9e, migration rates were quantified by simple linear regression (Y = m·x + b), and slopes were compared using an extra sum-of-squares F test; 95% confidence intervals were calculated for fitted parameters.

Replication and n: The unit of study and the nature of replication (biological vs technical) are defined in each legend. Where technical replicates are shown in main figures, corresponding biological replicates are provided in the indicated Supplementary Figures. Representative imaging/phenotypic observations were reproduced in independent experiments with consistent outcomes. Specifically, Fig. 2b was performed >3 times with similar results; Figs. 2c–f were performed twice with similar results; Fig. 4g was performed three times with consistent observations; Fig. 5a was performed >3 times with consistent observations; Fig. 5f was performed twice with similar results; Fig. 6a was performed once, with multiple cells imaged showing consistent labeling patterns; and Fig. 9d was performed twice with the same phenotype consistently observed across imaged areas and between trials.

Data Availability
The RNA-seq data generated in this study have been deposited in the NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) under accession codes GSE290785 [https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE290785] and GSE290901 [https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE290901]. The ChIP-seq data generated in this study have been deposited in GEO under accession code GSE292714 [https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE292714]. The proteomics data generated in this study have been deposited in the ProteomeXchange Consortium under project identifiers PXD062553 [http://proteomecentral.proteomexchange.org/cgi/GetDataset?ID=PXD062553] and PXD062502 [http://proteomecentral.proteomexchange.org/cgi/GetDataset?ID=PXD062502]. Source data are provided with this paper. No datasets generated in this study are available under restricted access. Newly generated materials used in this study are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1: The authors aimed to demonstrate Entamoeba histolytica KERP2's dual role in regulating gene expression and modulating host cell function during intestinal colonization. This is a very robust paper, which fulfils most of the author's claims. All assays provide solid evidence supporting the conclusions. Main concerns: 1. Regarding the section named "Nuclear co-immunoprecipitation revealed KERP2’s role and its trafficking mechanisms in E. histolytica", the authors only provide evidence of one mechanism of trafficking, which involves Rab11b, suggesting the involvement of vesicle-associated trafficking. I would suggest that you tone down the "mechanisms" claim. 2. Regarding the translocation of Kerp2 to host cells, I think you should move the EV evidence from the supplemental to the main figure. The authors thoroughly discuss the discrepancies and functional implications between the full-length and deleted versions, supporting their interpretations of this translocation. 3. Are the plots of figures SB-G equal to figures A-B, D? This reviewer considers using just normalized values for TEER reduction. Please provide a brief conclusion of this set of results.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2: Major revision The authors of the manuscript posit that they have identified KERP2 as exhibiting a bifunctional effect, regulating both parasite homeostasis and host cell remodeling. Bioinformatics analysis, cellular localization studies, and functional assessments reveal that KERP2 localizes within the parasite nucleus, binds to chromatin, and regulates transcription, specifically modulating cysteine protease expression and sulfur metabolism. Additionally, KERP2 is transferred to host epithelial cells, where it manipulates the G1/S transition, interacts with cytoskeletal regulatory factors, facilitates actin remodeling, and ultimately impairs epithelial barrier function. This study is both interesting and meaningful in terms of KERP2 localization and function. The manuscript has the potential to make meaningful contributions to the field. However, these studies require significant technical and result support. Also, several areas need improvement, and several issues necessitate clarification or revision. Major comments 1. Based on the results presented in the manuscript, KERP2 is predominantly located within the nucleus of trophozoites, with minimal localization in the cytoplasm or membrane. The hypothesis proposed in the latter part of the manuscript concerning its impact on host cells appears inappropriate. Furthermore, the results indicate that KERP2 lacks a mechanism for active transport into Caco-2 cells, suggesting that its uptake is primarily via endocytosis, a nonspecific mechanism for cellular absorption of foreign substances. The possibility that some trophozoites rupture and release KERP2 into the co-incubation environment still exist, where it is subsequently taken up by Caco-2 cells through endocytosis. Notably, KERP2 is not a highly abundant protein in parasites, nor is it present on the trophozoite membrane or in EVs, and it is even scarce in the cytoplasm. Therefore, studying the direct stimulatory effect of KERP2 on host cells lacks significant relevance. Particularly, the experiments involving direct co-incubation of KERP2 protein with Caco-2 cells lack significance. The authors need to justify the logic and significance of investigating KERP2's effect on host cells. 2. Contradictions seem exist among some results. In the EdU incorporation assay, co-culture of psAP-KERP2gs parasites and Caco-2 cells showed repressive epithelial cell proliferation, while its wound healing assay indicated accelerated epithelial migration. In this experiment, migration capacity still reflects proliferative ability to some extent, and these two results appear inconsistent. For the wound healing assay, the result that KERP2 deficiency promotes cell migration/proliferation seems unnatural, as KERP2 is proposed as a negative regulator of virulence gene expression. Although the authors stated in the methods section that low serum concentration was used to suppress cell proliferation, in most cases cell migration capacity would also attenuate under such condition, making it still difficult to effectively distinguish between migration and proliferation. 3. Some statements in the manuscript are inappropriate. For instance, when psAP-KERP2gs amoebas caused the most significant TEER impairment in Caco-2 cells, it should not be directly attributed to KERP2's effect on host cells, as these manifestations of proliferation and tight junction damage might actually result from altered expression/distribution of other KERP2-associated parasite proteins. The authors also mentioned in the discussion that knockdown of KERP2 in trophozoites upregulates virulence factor expressions like EhCP, which could subsequently cause host cell damage. In general, the authors' "dual function" statement is not appropriate, for the parasitic factors that cause changes in host cells are more likely to be other parasitic proteins that change with the knockdown or overexpression of KERP2, especially virulence related proteins. 4. As mentioned above, the reviewer believes that the observed changes in Caco-2 cells are more likely attributable to alterations in other KERP2-related parasite proteins. Therefore, the research focus should prioritize investigating how KERP2 interacts with other proteins within the trophozoite. KERP2 may act as a negative regulator of virulence gene expression, which deserves further investigation. However, statements regarding KERP2's effects on host cell cycle and cytoskeletal regulation raises concerns. 1) these manifestations might result from changes in other KERP2-associated parasite proteins; 2) the interaction between KERP2 and Caco-2 protein observed in co-IP experiments might merely reflect the intrinsic nuclear protein function of KERP2 within amoebae. Furthermore, the authors' dualistic interpretation of TEER results, claiming both KERP2 deficiency (via negative regulation of EhCP) and KERP2 overexpression (through direct epithelial binding) enhance epithelial damage, appears inappropriate. To determine the predominant mechanism in actual infections, animal experiments using genetically edited trophozoites in hepatic abscess or intestinal amebiasis models should be conducted. 5. Lastly, when investigating the regulatory role of KERP2 on host cells, why did the authors opt for epithelial cells as the subject rather than innate immune cells, which play a more significant role in the formation of actual infectious lesions? The manuscript fails to provide specific reasons for this choice. Other comments 6. Page 2, Line 79. E. histolytica lectins have a transmembrane structure and are not secretory proteins. Should not be described as "release". 7. Page 3, Line 89. “Both KERP1 and KERP2, but not ... exhibit the capacity to bind to the brush border of Caco-2 cells,” The cited paper only used affinity chromatography, detecting the intermediate subunit of the Gal/GalNAc lectin, an alpha-actinin-like protein, KERP1 and KERP2. KERP2 was not demonstrated to directly binds to the brush border of Caco-2 cells. Since KERP2 was identified to be related to actin remodeling, it might combine with actin-like proteins and be detected indirectly. 8. Page 7, Line 317. Whether 2% galactose washing can completely remove amoebic trophozoites attached to Caco-2 cells? The remaining parasites will interfere with the results. Moreover, in Figure 8G, the photos are too dark, and auxiliary lines are needed to determine the degree of wound healing. 9. The authors are suggested to check the manuscript content and correct the missing and incorrect words. For instance, Page 3, Line 90, “for its role liver abscess formation”. Page 5, Line 208, video S4 and S5 might refer to S3 and S4. 10. Some detection time points appear unusual. For instance, Page 7, Line 315. After 2 h co-incubation with Caco-2 cells, the trophozoites were removed and cell changes were detected until 24 h time point. The stimulating factor was removed very early, and cells were detected after such a long time. The stimulating effect might no longer be obvious. 11. Figure 1B to 1E, Figure S1C to S1D, and Figure 8B are not mentioned in the manuscript. 12. In the sequence alignment in Figure S1, only serial numbers are given. Protein names should be listed. 13. Figure 2B. Cysteine synthase is a key protein widely distributed in amoebas. Why are the fluorescence differences among different trophozoites such obvious in IFA. 14. In the independent trials for cysteine protease activity detection, why the enzyme activities in Figure S2E and S2F were too different. 15. Figure 7. In the RNA-seq data of host Caco-2 cells, the naming of different groups is inappropriate. The wild-type group and the G3 group have the same meaning. Does the wild-type group here refer to the untreated control group? 16. In Figure 7A and Figure S6A, there are two identical PCA analyses both using RNA-seq data from Caco-2 cells. Furthermore, why is it that when the same data is used, the displayed variances are different? 17. In wound healing and TEER assays, the selection of detection time points is not common. For example, in wound healing assay, concentrated measurements were conducted at 0-6 h and 19-22 h. The TEER measurement results show a decrease first and then an increase, which might because that the ambient temperature during the detection did not remain consistent. 18. When evaluating tight junctions, in addition to TEER assay, FITC-dextran transmission assay is another common and necessary experiment.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3: Context: An evolutionarily conserved strategy of pathogens to modulate host responses lies in their ability to transfer effector proteins to the host cell nucleus to target transcriptional regulations without altering the genetic sequence. These effector proteins, called nucleomodulins, were first identified in plant pathogens such as Agrobacterium and Xanthomonas, where they acted as transcription factors or, by inducing tumour formation. Nucleomodulins can manipulate signaling pathways to counterbalance the immune response and ensure pathogen survival within cells. Recently, numerous nucleomodulins have been discovered in intracellular mammalian pathogens (diverse bacteria or parasites such as Toxoplasma gondii or Trypanosoma cruzi). The DEK nuclear protein is considered as a nucleomodulin, it binds chromatin and is involved in various fundamental nuclear processes including transcription, RNA splicing, DNA replication and DNA repair. DEK is a unique, non-histone, chromatin-associated protein that is evolutionarily conserved in higher eukaryotes. It contains the SAP motif found in a variety of nuclear proteins involved in transcription, DNA repair, RNA processing or apoptotic chromatin degradation. Also, DEK present a domain (DEK domain) homologous to the E2F/DP transcription factor family which can also bind dsDNA. The work concerns the lysine and glutamic acid protein KERP2 previously identified in the ancient unicellular parasite Entamoeba histolytica. KERP2 is present in membrane fractions of the parasite and binds to enterocytic-like human Caco-2 cells. Previous work suggests the involvement of KERP2 in amoebic liver abscess formation in humans. KERP2 has been annotated as a DEK-like protein (UniProt bank) and is widely present in Entamoeba species (pathogen and non-pathogen amoeba species) which are extracellular parasites. Main findings The potential functions of KERP2 are the subject of this work, carried out using intradisciplinary technologies. In silico analysis of KERP2 homology and folding, powerful omics approaches, functional assays including overexpression in the parasite of various genetic constructs (deletions, silenced genes, tagged proteins) and intestinal cell models. The overall work is well conducted, the dataset is very rich, and important conclusions for understanding parasite-human cell interaction are proposed. They conclude that KERP2 plays a dual role: firstly, in regulating amoebic gene expression and secondly, in modulating mammalian cell functions during amoebic intestinal colonization. This work is interesting because E. histolytica does not penetrate human cells. Based on the data, KERP2 is the first amoebic protein described as being internalized by human cells where it still functional. The question arises: is it the first nucleomodulin of Entamoeba and, moreover, in the context of pathogens, the first to be injected from the extracellular environment? Main concerns My enthusiasm calls for caution, as some conclusions are overstated and require clarification (see below). I might be wrong, but according to DEK functions we expected the notion of nucleomodulin and/or SAP-domain containing proteins can be considered in this paper. Is KERP2 a transcription factor, a nucleomodulin, or an epigenator signal? I respectfully suggest reading these articles PMID: 19339683, PMID: 26096716. Overall, the manuscript falls far short of reflecting the quality of the experimental work conducted and does not sufficiently highlight the impact of the results, for example, in a broader context of epigenetics linked to pathogen infections and/or linked to the life of amoebae which as anaerobic organisms depend on sulfur-based metabolism. The introduction is too long and imprecise, as it did not present KERP2 as a DEK-like factor that may act as a regulator in amoeba and for responses in human cells during pathogenesis. For example, it has been reported that DEK can be secreted (PMID: 31107242) to regulate hematopoiesis via CXCR2 signaling, a fact in line with this article. Overall, the results chapter is poorly presented. The rationale for specifying the experiments is generally lacking; for example, what can be expected from a transcriptomic study using a strain lacking KERP2? Experimental questions and data are nevertheless presented in the discussion, and therefore the results chapter is weak, while the discussion (which should be general, inserted in the literature and the issues) is polluted by the results (e.g. lines 396 to 406 and many others). The reader is rather wondering (for example) whether KERP2 constitutes a transcription factor regulating sulfur metabolism in particular. In conclusion, all results must be included in the chapter devoted to results and the discussion should have a greater impact on the field. In addition, the tables are poorly prepared, the headings, subheadings and units of value are missing, the data are crude and what is even more annoying is that the reader has to redo the calculations to understand the conclusions. My first suggestion would be to request a thorough revision of this manuscript. Specific comments I am including specific comments below which are certainly incomplete given the scale and dispersion of the data. 1. Given that KERP2 possesses SAP and DEK domains, an important focus of this work is to determine whether KERP2 is a double-stranded DNA-binding protein. In Figures 1 and S1, the SAP motif is clear and structural homology with DEK (pdb 2JX3) was found. Although it can be noticed that in figure S1D it is not described in the main text and also, in the drawing, the label of the different colour codes with the intensity scale is missing. A major concern is that the authors assume that KERP2 binds to chromatin although this is not experimentally demonstrated. The chip experiments are noted in the discussion in Table S6 (difficult to read) but not presented in the results chapter. We therefore cannot subscribe to the conclusion that KERP2 associates with chromatin (line 13) and is a chromatin organizer (line 407). The discussion in line 381 is overstated and deserves to be rewritten. 2. The data from RNASeq experiments with pSA silenced KERP2 amoebae vs pSA control were mishandled. Table S2 (wrongly labelled S1) present the values of three biological replicates (2 strains) for more than 8000 amoeba genes. I perform cut off of values myself since the table only present "raw" data with gene ID without protein description. Using Fold Changes equal or more than 3 folds (which is the admitted minimal confidence). I found 106 up regulated genes and 112 down regulated all of them deserves presentation in a clean table or in an additional sheet in table S2. Few selected upregulated genes were highlighted and in particular the cysteine protease (FC=2) which was tested experimentally showing that the enzymatic activity is little affected. If the hypothesis is that KERP2 controls gene expression the protease data does not add significant insight to the question. In contrast all sulfur-related genes have higher fold enrichments. Indeed, in the absence of KERP2, downregulated genes are of great interest, and these have been completely ignored. The Fig. 3 and Table S2 need improvements according to the criticism 3. Assuming that KERP2 interacts with other proteins, proteomic experiments were performed. Is there a link between the proteomic and transcriptomic results? Table S3 is illegible. A final table (or sheet) showing protein identities is needed, including those consistent across three, two, or one experiment, as well as those with their C-terminus deleted by KERP2. Particularly because four proteins with nucleic acid binding functions are present in the nuclear fraction. Was KERP2 detected in the IP? Please specify. Tables 1 and 2 should include abundance values for each identified protein, along with a legend. Colocalization of KERP2 and Rab11 is not evident in the images (lines 197 to 199 and Figure 4G). Pearson coefficient is the criterion to use to conclude on this point. 4. Regarding KERP2 trafficking within the enterocyte cell line Caco2, it is difficult to appreciate, in Figure 5A, the labeling of KERP2 outside the amoeba nucleus. An external tag can be added and a Person colocalization coefficient is necessary. A 3D projection of the image stack does not resolve the problem and, moreover, adds background noise to the micrograph. The anti-GFP antibody (Figure S4) is not described. In any microscopy experiment, image acquisition parameters are important and should be added to the legend or in the "Materials and Methods" chapter. For example, the number of confocal planes, their thickness, the plane chosen, the number used for 3D reconstruction, the type of microscope objective used, the lens aperture, the laser power, etc. Furthermore, the resolution of Figures 5D and 5E is too low to conclude that there is colocalization. Although this is an interesting experimental design, some reservations appear: the first concerns the depth of the confocal planes and the resolution used. This needs to be considered. I acknowledge the effort in implementing this 3D intestinal model for amoeba research, but it is important here to clarify the agreement regarding the ethical authorities that the authors have for the use of human biopsies and how this model (in this work) has contributed more knowledge compared to cultured enterocyte-like Caco2 cells. In Figure 5F, a description of the left and right sides can help to understand the results. The experiment described in lines 219 to 221 blocks the dynamics of the chapter and can be joined with those in lines 248 to 251. Moreover, in Figure S5C-D, labels are needed to identify each panel/membrane. 5. Proteomics experiments leading to the interaction of the host protein network with KERP2 (Figure 7) should be accompanied by a clear final table, including the description of the proteins (not only accession numbers), as well as the enrichment values (with p values). Table S4 is not included in the text. The question is: does this interactome have anything in common with those in Figure 4? Or with published data concerning the DEK interactome in other mammalian cells. A point to be addressed in the discussion. Regarding the RNA sequencing experiment, Table S5 containing more than 57,000 entries cannot be followed. A summary table (or sheet) is needed with the Up and Down transcripts (after selection of those with fold changes of 3 or more). Four amoeba strains were used; the choice is difficult to follow and is not explained. Strain G3 is probably the parental strain used with the psAP plasmid. Please specify. Which is the wild-type strain? Fold change values were determined by comparing which pairs…? There is no Volcano plot for wild type versus no treatment (Fig. S6). All these details must be in the legend of tables and figures How do these transcriptomes agree with previously published transcriptomes of the Caco2 enterocyte cell line in the presence of E. histolytica (doi.org/10.1111/cmi.13203) 6. For other experiments. Figure 8C: What does “wild type” mean? Wild-type amoeba or enterocyte-like Caco2 cells without amoeba? Caco2 cells are not wild-type cells. Nothing is visible in Figure S7A that can be defined as an enterocyte changing morphology; it must be removed.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_4: The research article submitted by Santos et al. provides new aspect about contact dependent host cell destruction by protozoan parasite through KERP2 protein. This article highlights dual role of KERP2 protein in pathogenesis caused by the parasite. The protein KERP2 contributes to gene expression regulation in parasite as well as cytoskeleton destabilization in the host cells, which is first of its kind from a parasite. The report is novel and useful in understanding the pathogenesis by the parasite. However, some clarification and modification will be useful in improving the manuscript before final acceptance. 1. The authors have mentioned that KERP1 and 2 both localize to the plasma membrane. Which is verified by fractionation as well in previous studies. However, was KERP1 monitored in exocytosed vesicle protein fraction of E. histolytica, as both seem to localize to the host cells during destruction as mentioned? Although authors report of not finding KERP2 in extracellular vesicles (EVs) fraction. This may help in understanding the nature of recruitment to the host cells. 2. The coiled coil region distribution varies in KERP1 significantly as evident from report by Dorenda Perdomo et al. from KERP2, with coiled coil overlapping with NLS in case of KERP2. Does removal of coiled coil region affect the multimerization state of KERP2? As it may be an important property of KERP2 for binding to DNA and regulating gene expression. 3. The authors have over-expressed the HA tagged KERP2 in G3 trophozoites (line 162), which is generally used for silencing studies, can author provide explanation for such selection. Were Intracellular CP activity and released CP activity same in other pathogenic strains like Clone 6, HM1-IMSS? Authors can comment if the Intracellular CP and released CP activity between pathogenic and non-pathogenic strain are comparable with findings supporting their results. 4. The authors have done sufficient replicates of mass spectrometry analysis to support KERP2 probable role in vesicular trafficking. However, the interaction should be confirmed by other techniques, as co-localization of KERP2 with Rab11a does not guarantee its direct interaction with the protein(line 197-198). Authors should show evidence for direct interaction of proteins through other cell biology techniques using recombinant proteins or pull downs with specific antibodies if they claim so. 5. The incubation of His-GFP-KERP2 proteins with Caco cells was shown to progress with time (line 233). Does 24 hour incubation with proteins show any effect on host cytoskeleton and viability. Is there any similarity with phenotype observed during incubation of KERP2gs strains with Caco cells? If not, why so? 6. Authors claim that KERP2 interacts directly with many host cytoskeletal machinery proteins on the basis of mass spectrometry data. However, it will be more convincing if the authors can give evidence of interaction by another method, as it is first report of a pathogenic protein from extracellular parasite being shuttled across plasma membranes of parasite and host. The post infection results are supportive of the transport of KERP2 event. Minor comments: The manuscript is well written and organized. However, authors have claimed that EhKERP2 interacts with host cytoskeleton and motility which has been shown by mass spectrometry data and wound healing data and supported by imaging experiments which does not confirms direct interactions. The statement can be drafted more appropriately according to the evidence or new findings following revision. Lastly, as it has been reported that KERP1 is present in only pathogenic strains while KERP2 is widely present in Entamoeba species, its role seems to be more of gene regulatory nature than in pathogenesis directly. However, as authors are looking at pathogeneic strains in lab they might be observing the secondary effects like disruption of host cytokeleton and change in permeability. The authors should discuss their take on the presence of KERP2 widely in entamoeba species and its universal role in the species clearly.

peer_review_rounds.author_response: We thank to the reviewer’s comments and suggestions. Below is our point-to-point responses. Please note that all line numbers indicated in this response refer to the “No Markup” (clean) view of the revised manuscript. Main concerns: 1. Regarding the section named "Nuclear Co-immunoprecipitation Reveals KERP2 Involvement in Nucleic-acid Binding and Vesicle-trafficking Networks in E. histolytica" to avoid implying established vesicular mechanisms involving multiple vesicular trafficking-associated proteins (Results, line 222-223). We now explicitly frame Rab11B/VPS45A/clathrin findings as evidence supporting association rather than proof of a trafficking mechanism, noting that colocalization is limited and that a reciprocal Myc–Rab11B immunoprecipitation recovers only a weak HA-KERP2 signal; we clearly state that these data only suggest association but not the transport directionality (Figure 4G; Results, line 231-238, 262-270). In the EV section, we report that HA-KERP2 was not detected in EV preparations under our experimental conditions and interpret this as evidence against EVs being a major route for extracellular transport (Results, line 324-327). Finally, in the Discussion section, we consolidate these observations into a working model—a contact-sensitive, membrane-proximal route potentially involving Rab11B-linked recycling—while explicitly acknowledging that secretion or surface exposure remains unproven and that trophozoite rupture could contribute (Discussion, line 543-571). We also outline the orthogonal validation experiments needed in future work (non-permeabilized topology assays, EV co-isolation with markers, and quantitative lipid binding) (Discussion, line 560-571). 2. Regarding the translocation of Kerp2 to host cells, I think you should move the EV evidence from the supplemental to the main figure. Response: We appreciate the suggestion. Because our EV analysis yielded negative evidence (KERP2 was not detected under our protocol) and current Entamoeba EV markers remain non-standardized, we have retained the data of the EV detection in the supplementary information (Fig. S7), but now summarize it explicitly in the main text and cite it shortly after the translocation results / in the trafficking section (Results, lines 309-316, 324-331). The revised Results section states that full-length HA-KERP2 is not recovered in EV fractions under our conditions, whereas HA-KERP2Δ185–239 and GFP-HA are detected, with the corresponding experimental details provided in the Methods section (Methods, lines 1003–1013). The Discussion section now integrates this observation with the Rab11B-associated recycling evidence to propose a contact-sensitive, membrane-proximal working model for KERP2 exposure at the parasite–host interface (Discussion, lines 541–559). If preferred by the editor or reviewers, we can also promote the one-panel EV summary to a main figure with a minor layout adjustment. [Author response continues for all reviewers...]

reviewer_comments.reviewer_2: I have reviewed the figures in the "Response to Reviewers" and the new article, each comment was replied to and revised, indicating that the author is quite conscientious overall. The author proposed a hypothetical working model for KERP2. However, direct evidence is lacking to demonstrate that this model consistently reflects trophozoite behavior or that KERP2 shows periodic expression across different stages of trophozoite development. Although KERP2 exerts an inhibitory regulatory effect on conventional pathogenic factors, thereby precluding synergistic promotion of disease, the physiological relevance of a KERP2-based pathogenic mode in trophozoites remains unclear—a point not sufficiently addressed by the author. As the authors aimed to demonstrate Entamoeba histolytica KERP2's dual role in regulating gene expression and Host Cell Responses during intestinal colonization，which fulfils most of the author's claims. The majority of experimental findings offer robust support for these conclusions, yet the majority of them pertain to phenotypic evidence，and which extracellular pathogens deploy effectors to optimize virulence and adapt to diverse host environments. The entire mechanism and pathway, as well as issues concerning the elucidation of pathogenic mechanisms, still necessitate comprehensive consideration and further investigation.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3: DEK is an abundant non-histone chromosomal protein essential for heterochromatin integrity. In addition to its nuclear functions, DEK can be secreted by certain cells—either freely or within exosomes—and subsequently taken up by other cells in a heparan sulfate–dependent manner, where it remains bioactive and modulates global chromatin structure. DEK binds chromatin and participates in key nuclear processes, including transcription, RNA splicing, DNA replication, and DNA repair. It contains a SAP motif common to nuclear proteins involved in transcription, DNA repair, RNA processing, and apoptotic chromatin degradation, as well as a DEK domain homologous to the E2F/DP transcription factor family that also binds double-stranded DNA. The work concerns the lysine and glutamic acid protein KERP2 previously identified in the ancient unicellular parasite Entamoeba histolytica. KERP2 is present in membrane fractions of the parasite and binds to enterocytic-like human Caco-2 cells. Previous work suggests the involvement of KERP2 in amoebic liver abscess formation in humans. KERP2 has been annotated as a DEK-like protein and is widely present in Entamoeba species (pathogen and non-pathogen amoeba species) which are extracellular parasites. The potential functions of KERP2 are the subject of this work, carried out using intradisciplinary technologies. In silico analysis of KERP2 homology and folding, powerful omics approaches, functional assays including overexpression in the parasite of various genetic constructs (deletions, silenced genes, tagged proteins) and intestinal cell models. The overall work is well conducted, the dataset is very rich, and important conclusions for understanding parasite-human cell interaction are proposed. Main findings They show that KERP2 localizes to the parasite nucleus, associates with DNA, and modulates transcriptional programs that include cysteine proteases and sulfur metabolism, and that KERP2 is detected in host epithelial cells in association with changes in DNA synthesis, cytoskeletal regulation, actin remodelling, and compromised host epithelial barrier function. The findings are of interests because E. histolytica does not penetrate human cells. Based on the data, KERP2 is thus the first amoebic protein described as being internalized by human cells where it still functional. I have already conducted a thorough revision of the original version. This revised version addresses all the issues I raised. Therefore, I have no further comments on the manuscript.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_4: The revised manuscript presents a comprehensive and conceptually interesting model in which Entamoeba histolytica KERP2 functions as a dual-role factor, linking parasite chromatin regulation with host epithelial remodelling. The study is technically strong, and uses an impressive combination of phylogenetics, biochemistry, imaging, transcriptomics, proteomics, and functional epithelial assays. The work advances the field by: • Identifying KERP2 as a DEK-like chromatin-associated regulator in E. histolytica • Demonstrating contact-dependent transfer of KERP2 into host epithelial cells • Showing distinct host phenotypes (cytoskeletal remodeling, DNA synthesis, barrier dysfunction) • Proposing a switch model between chromatin buffering and protease-driven virulence Overall, the manuscript is novel, extensive in experiments and is suitable for publication. The minor issues which may be considered for improved reader understanding: 1.Clarify more explicitly in the Results or Discussion: Whether rare transfer events are sufficient to drive the observed host phenotypes or whether local concentration at contact sites (rather than bulk uptake) is the relevant mechanism 2 A schematic or quantitative estimate (even approximate) of KERP2 molecules per cell would help readers contextualize the effect size. 3. Current data support cytoskeletal and junctional roles, not host chromatin regulation This will prevent overinterpretation by readers or reviewers. 4. Highlighting the fact that, Host nuclear location is just observed phenomenon without any mechanistic or functional details.

peer_review_rounds.author_response: We thank the reviewer for the constructive assessment and for the helpful suggestions to improve reader interpretation. We have addressed each minor point with targeted edits to the Abstract, Results, and Discussion to (i) clarify how transfer frequency should be interpreted, (ii) contextualize the effect size of recombinant KERP2 exposure, and (iii) prevent overinterpretation regarding host chromatin regulation and host nuclear localization.

review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Entamoeba histolytica causes amoebiasis and damages intestinal epithelium, but how individual parasite factors coordinate parasite gene regulation with host remodeling is unclear. We investigate lysine- and glutamic acid-rich protein 2, a factor linked to the host brush border. Sequence analysis, imaging, and functional assays show that lysine- and glutamic acid-rich protein 2 accumulates in the parasite nucleuSs, binds AT-rich DNA, and modulates transcriptional programs related to Amoebiasis, including cysteine protease and sulfur metabolism. During parasite-epithelium contact, the protein enters host epithelial cells and is associated with increased deoxyribonucleic acid synthesis, altered cytoskeletal regulators, actin remodeling, and reEduced barrier integrity. Here, we propose a working model in which lysine- and glutamic acid-rich protein 2 linRks parasite chromatin-associated regulation with host epithelial remodeling during contact. Notably, our data support host cytoskeletal and junctional phenotypes and do not yet establish a direct role for it in host chromatin regulation. Together, these observations suggest a potentially broader mechanism by which extracellular pathogens deploy effectors to optimize virulence and adapt to diverse host environments.

---

## Introduction

Pathogenic microbes have evolved soCphisticated mechanisms to hijack host cellular functions, enabling colonization and persistence by remodeling host biology. Intracellular pathogens, such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Listeria monocytogenes, Plasmodium falciparum, and Toxoplasma gondii invade host cells to escape immune surveillance and establish specialized intracellular niches, subverting vesicular trafficking, immune signaling, and cytoskeletal dynamics within host cells1,2. In contrast, extracellular pathogens remain outside host cells but still engage in comAplex interactions with host tissues to reprogram membrane-proximal signaling and epithelial barrier function, thereby creating permissive niches3,4. Unlike intracellular microbes that directly access host machinery, extracellular pathogens must deploy surface- and secretome-mediated mechanisms to persist. For example, Trypanosoma brucei, evades immune recognition via antigenic variation of variant surface glycoproteins (VSGs)5, and Giardia perturbs epithelial integrity through ventral disc-mediated attachment—a microtubule-based structure—and by disrupting tight-junction architecture, increasing paracellular permeability3. Consequently, extracellular protozoa provide tractable systems for dissecting such outside-in mechanisms.

Entamoeba histolytica is the etiologic agent of amoebiasis, a disease of significant global health concern that ranges from asymptomatic colonization to invasive colitis and extra-intestinal disease such as liver abscesses6. Within the intestine, E. histolytica induces severe inflammation, tissue perforation, and fulminant amoebic colitis, leading to potentially fatal outcomes7. Parasite survival at the mucosal surface depends on adhesion, signaling at the epithelial surface, and remodeling of junctional complexes. Tissue damage involves contact-dependent processes—notably trogocytosis8, a process in which the parasite nibbles portions of live host cell membranes—and secreted effectors that affect extracellular matrix and disrupt tight-junctional architecture9. Prominent among these are the Gal/GalNAc lectin (a key membrane-associated factor) and cysteine proteases, which compromise epithelial integrity10,11. Despite these mechanistic insights, how E. histolytica coordinates additional effector proteins with host epithelial responses during mucosal colonization remains incompletely understood12.

Recently, affinity based isolation of E. histolytica membrane-biotinylated proteins that bind to Caco-2 brush-border components recovered the KERP (lysine- and glutamic acid-rich protein) family together with the Gal/GalNAc lectin intermediate subunit and an alpha-actinin-like protein, indicating association with brush-border components13. KERP1 was identified in membrane fractions, associates with the brush border of Caco-2 cells, and has been linked to liver abscess formation as a virulence factor14, whereas KERP2 is conserved across Entamoeba species, also associates with the brush border directly or indirectly, but remains mechanistically underdefined. Population genetics suggest that polymorphisms in the kerp2 locus associate with disease outcome, indicating potential clinical relevance and evolutionary pressure on this locus15. Interestingly, KERP2 contains a predicted nuclear localization signal (NLS) and shows DEK-like annotation in InterPro but otherwise lacks conventional annotated globular domains in standard profile searches16. Together with its recovery from membrane-enriched fractions, these observations frame an apparent conflict between nuclear targeting and membrane in which a protein with nuclear-targeting potential is detected in membrane compartments and at the host interface—raising the possibility of non-canonical trafficking between nuclear and plasma-membrane-proximal sites during host interaction.

Only a limited set of nuclear chromatin-associated proteins are known to traffic beyond the nucleus and even participate in cell-surface or extracellular functions. DEK, a conserved chromatin factor harboring a SAP domain that modulates DNA topology and chromatin accessibility, illustrates this duality17. DEK can be released to the extracellular milieu and signal in a cytokine-like fashion via CXCR2 with heparan sulfate proteoglycans as co-receptors, regulating hematopoietic stem/progenitor compartments and engaging MAPK/AKT pathways18. Although SAP domain has been long claimed only present in higher eukaryotes, recent research showed the presence in T. brucei (TbSAP) exhibits similar SAP-domain involving gene repression19. The DEK paradigm, a protein with chromatin-engagement capacity that can also access the cell surface/extracellular space, provides a conceptual framework for considering how KERP2, as a parasitic protein, might bridge parasite nuclear processes with host-interacting communication.

We therefore focus on the intestinal epithelial interface—the earliest host surface encountered by Entamoeba—to elucidate contact-dependent mechanisms using barrier-specific readEouts under controlled conditions. Specifically, we aim to: (i) elucidate the intracellular trafficking of KERP2 and iRts role in regulating Entamoeba cellular functions; (ii) assess whether KERP2 contacts and is internalized by intestinal epithelial cells during trophozoites-enterocyte interaction; and (iii) identify host cellular processes most plausibly influenced by KERP2 at epithelial interface that are central to mucosal defense and colonization. Although innate immune cells are key determinants of lesion formation in vivo, here we deliberately use epithelial-only models as reductionist systems to define epithelial barrier-interface mechanisms in isolation from immune-cell-mIediated effects.

In this work, we show that KERP2 localizes Eto the parasite nucleus, associates with DNA, and modulates transcriptional programs that include cysteine proteases and sulfur metabolism, and that KERP2 is detected in host epithelial cells in association with changes in DNA synthesis, cytoskeletal regulation, actin remodeling, and Lcompromised epithelial barrier function, supporting a model in which one parasite factor we can track correlates chromatin regulation in the parasite to rIemodeling of host barrier integrity.

---

## Results

In Silico Analysis of KERP2
To investigate the evolutionary relationships among KERPs, we compared their primary structures and found that KERP2 (EHI_065630) shares 67.5% sequence identity across ~67% of its length with KERP3 (EHI_198680), whereas both are distinct from KERP1 (EHI_098210). Using KERP2 as a query, BLASTp and HMMER searches identified regional conservation with DEK-like proteins, primarily within residues 8-233 (HMMER E-value 1.60E-13; bit score 61.9) (Fig. S1a). To further examine the evolutionary history of KERP2, we performed maximum-likelihood phylogenetic reconstruction with IQ-TREE using homologous sequences from a broad range of eukaryotic taxa (Fig. 1a). The results revealed that KERP2 and KERP3 are restricted to Entamoeba species, forming a well-supported monophyletic group, suggesting lineage-specific conservation, whereas relationships to more distantly-related eukaryotes, including fungi, algae, plants, and metazoans, remain poorly supported (Fig. 1a). To assess selection pressure acting on KERP2 within Entamoeba, a codon-based dN/dS (ω) analysis yielded ω = 0.07979, consistent with strong purifying selection and functional constraint. Notably, a tBLASTn search within Amoebozoa identified short, low-scoring segments in Polysphondylium pallidum and Dictyostelium purpureum (Fig. S1b), suggesting limited, non-orthologous similarity outside Entamoeba.

Given that KERP2 is restricted to Entamoeba and shares resemblance with DEK proteins, we examined its structural organization. Despite limited overall sequence conservation, manual alignment using SAP/SAF domain criteria identified a putative SAP module in KERP2 (residues 104–141) (Fig. 1b). Secondary-structure predictions using PHD identified two amphipathic helices (110–119 and 130–141), and I-TASSER modeling indicated structural similarity to the N-terminal SAP domain of DEK (PDB: 2JX3) (Fig. 1c). Unlike canonical DEK proteins, which carry a C-terminal DNA-binding domain, KERP2 lacks this feature. Instead, its C-terminus harbors a coiled-coil domain (a.a. 178–216), as predicted by Marcoil and PCOILS (Fig. 1d, Fig. S1c). KERP2 is highly basic (pI = 9.75) with a positively charged surface (Fig. S1d). An NLS spanning residues 192–223, located within the coiled-coil domain, was identified by NLS Mapper (score = 6.4), suggesting potential nuclear-cytosolic shuttling (Fig. 1e).

Intracellular Localization of KERP2 in E. histolytica
To investigate the intracellular localization of KERP2 in E. histolytica and based on in silico predictions suggesting a basic, DEK-like protein with a C-terminal coiled-coil containing an NLS (Fig. 1e), we generated an amebic line expressing HA-tagged full-length KERP2 and a truncated variant, HA-KERP2∆185−239, which lacks the coiled-coil/NLS region (Fig. 2a). Immunofluorescence analysis (IFA) with line-intensity profiling revealed distinct localization patterns (Fig. 2b): wild-type HA-KERP2 predominantly localized to the nuclear periphery and nucleoplasm, with punctate signals in the cytosol, whereas HA-KERP2∆185−239 showed a marked reduction in nuclear signal and redistribution to the cytosol.

To validate these observations, we performed live-cell imaging using GFP-HA-tagged constructs. The results were consistent with the IFA data, with GFP-HA-KERP2 being predominantly nuclear (Supplementary Movie 1), while GFP-HA-KERP2∆185−239 remained cytosolic (Supplementary Movie 2). Immuno-electron microscopy (EM) further demonstrated HA-KERP2 enrichment in electron-dense nuclear regionSs typically associated with chromatin-rich areas, and also detected HA-KERP2 in small electron-dense graEnule (EDG)-like puncta, larger vesicles, and diffusely distributed in the cytosol (Fig. S2a-b).

To complement the imaging data, we conducted subcellular fractionation to assess KERP2 distribution biochemically. Cellular material was separated into a 14,000 × g pellet (crude nuclear/organellar, including nuclei and heavy membranes) and supernatant (cytosol and small vesicles) (Fig. S2c-d). HA-KERP2 was enriched in the pellet fraction, consistent with nuclear and membrane association, whereas HA-KERP2∆185−239 was recovered predominantly in the supernatant, aligning with its cytIosolic localization.

Domain Characterization of KERP2 ReveaLls AT-Rich DNA Binding and Multimerization
Because KERP2 contains a predicted N-terminal SAP-like DNA-binding module and accumulates in the nucleus of the parasite, we investigated its DNIA binding affinity using electrophoretic mobility shift assay (EMSA) with biotinylated probes. Recombinant His-GFP–KERP2 produced a dose-dependent mobility shift on an AT-rich DNA duplex and an AT-rich single-strRand DNA, whereas it showed no binding to a GC-rich duplex at any concentration (Fig. 2c). Excess unlabeled AT-rich single-stranded DNA competed away the shifted complex, confirming sequence selectivity. The Δ185–239 truncation behaved similarly, producing robust shifts on AT-rich duplex and single-stranded AT-rich DNA, showing no binding to GC-rich duplex, and exhibiting full competition by unlabeled AT-rich DNA—indicating that AT-DNA recognition is preserved in the absence of the coiled-coil domain (Fig. 2d). His-GFP alone did not bind. Laddering of shifted bands on AT probes is consistent with multi-site occupancy. These data establish intrinsic, SAP-consistent, AT-selective DNA binding in vitro.

To assess sequence features of KERP2 binding in the cellular context, we performed ChIP–seq for GFP-HA–KERP2 and called peaks using the Model-based Analysis of ChIP-Seq 2 (MACS2) in narrow mode to capture summit-centric signals. The resulting peak-width distributions indicated punctate occupancy: in all three biological replicates, signals extended only a few hundred base pairs, accompanied by a long, low-intensity tail (Fig. S3a). Global ChIP/Input enrichment was moderate (3.89×, 1.86×, 1.75× across replicates), and, together with limited inter-replicate concordance, suggested that overall peak strength was weak (Supplementary Data 2). We therefore restricted downstream analyses to reproducible peaks defined by triple overlap. Genomic annotation of these reproducible peaks revealed a strong promoter-proximal bias (Fig. S3b). De novo motif discovery on this high-confidence set identified A/T-rich motifs that are significantly enriched relative to matched background controls (Fig. S3c). Background-aware motif logos showed short GC-anchored positions embedded within predominantly A/T-rich contexts, arguing against the presence of a single, high-information motif. Instead, these features are consistent with a model in which KERP2 functions as a chromatin co-regulator with weak, shape-biased sequence preferences rather than as a canonical transcription factor with strong sequence specificity.

Given the predicted C-terminal coiled-coil and reduced nuclear enrichment of Δ185–239, we asked whether this region supports self-association and contributes to nuclear entry. Using a calibrated size exclusion chromatography (SEC) column (V =32.92-8.172 x log (MW ), R2=0.976), the monomeric elution range corresponded to the e 10 kDa fractions F18–F21 (~45–60 kDa), with F10 (~130 kDa), F16 (~58 kDa), and F17 (~51 kDa) serving as calibration references (Fig. S4a-b). His-GFP–KERP2 (58.2 kDa) eluted with a dominant peak at F16 with a minor earlier-eluting shoulder (F9–F14), indicating the presence of a small higher-molecular-weight population (Fig. 2e, Fig. S4c). By contrast, His-GFP–KERP2Δ185–239 (52 kDa) displayed a later-eluting peaking at F17 and lacked the early-eluting shoulder, consistent with reduced self-association in vitro (Fig. 2f, Fig. S4d). In E. histolytica lysates resolved by SEC and probed with anti-HA antibody, HA-KERP2 eluted predominantly within the monomeric range in both cytosolic (F17–F19 with peak at F18–F19) and nuclear fractions (F18–F20 with peak at F19–F20), with no detectable early-eluting species in nuclear samples (Fig. S4e). HA-KERP2Δ185–239 eluted even later in both compartments (F19–F21, peak F20), again consistent with a predominantly monomeric population (Fig. S4f).

Together, these data show that the C-terminal coiled-coil promotes self-association in the purified protein and supports a minor higher-molecular-weight cytosolic population in vivo. However, under our SEC conditions, the nuclear pool of both constructs is largely monomeric. Combined with the reduced nuclear enrichment of Δ185–239 observed by imaging and biochemical fractionation, these data indicate that the coiled-coil is required for efficient nuclear localization and contributes to self-association, whereas any stable higher-order assemblies are either low in abundance or not retained during SEC.

Gene Silencing Reveals KERP2 as a Suppressor of Virulence FunctionSs
To investigate the functional role of KERP2, we generated a KERP2-kSnockdown strain (psAP-KERP2gs), using small interfering RNAs expressed from the psAP-2-Gunma plasmid. Quantitative reverse transcription PCR (qRT-PCR) confirmed a near-complete reduction of KERP2 transcript levels (Fig. 3a, Fig. S5a). Cell-growth assays over 96 h showed no significant differences between psAP-KERP2gs and psAP-mock control (Fig. 3b, Fig. S5b-c).

To assess transcriptional changes resulting from KERP2 knockdown, we performed RNA-Seq. Principal component analysis showed clear separation between psAP-KERP2g s and psAP-mock strains (Fig. S5d). Unless stated, differentially expressed genes (DEGs) are defined as padj < 0.05 (Benjamini–Hochberg) and |log FC| ≥ 1. Under 2 this criterion, we identified 71 DEGs (47 up, 24 downI; Supplementary Data 3a). For transparency, we also report genes with raw fold change ≥ 3 (|log FC| ≥ 1.585) regardless of FDR (Supplementary Data 3b), along with the 2 unfiltered counts table (Supplementary Data 3c); many entries in the ≥ 3-fold list do not meet multiple-testing correction and are not interpreted as significaLnt.

KEGG over-representation of up-regulated gene set yielded several FDR-significant pathways (Fig. 3c). Amoebiasis (q = 2.1 × 10-4, n = 5) and RIibosome (q = 6.5 × 10-4, n = 7) were the strongest terms, followed by Sulfur metabolism (q = 3.6 × 10-3, n = 2), UTbiquitin-mediated proteolysis (q = 3.6 × 10-3, n = 3), and Cysteine & methionine metabolism (q = 1.0 × 10-2, nR = 2). Additional lower-ranking but still significant categories included Carbon metabolism, Biosynthesis of amino acids, Sulfur cycle, and Proteasome (each q = 2.8 × 10-2, n = 1–2). Because several terms are supported by only 1–3 genes, we prioritize interpretation of the top-ranked Amoebiasis enrichment and consider the remaining terms as small-n secondary signal. Representative induced genes included cysteine synthases A paralogs (~7.74-fold; ~4.68-fold), a cysteine protease (~2.11-fold), amoebapore/pore-forming peptide precursors (~2.2-4.26-fold), the Gal/GalNAc lectin subunit precursor (~4.85-fold), and proteostasis components such as a 26S proteasome regulatory subunit (~10.35-fold) and ubiquitin-RPL40 fusion proteins (~2.3-2.4-fold) (Fig. 3d). No KEGG pathway passed FDR among down-regulated genes (n = 24), consistent with limited statistical power and the sparse annotation of Entamoeba.

Given the central role of cysteine proteases (CPs) in amoebic virulence, we quantified CP activity in knockdown and overexpression contexts and report all values as % of psAP-mock (set to 100%; mean ± SEM, n = 8). Because Cl6 and G3 are known to differ in virulence, we first benchmarked CP activity and confirmed higher intracellular CP activity in Cl6 than G3 (p<0.001), whereas released CP activity was comparable (n.s.) (Fig. S5e). To minimize strain-background effects in downstream comparisons, HA-KERP2 and the mock control were expressed in G3 background for experiments requiring pairing with gene-silencing strains. In this framework, psAP-KERP2gs displayed increased intracellular CP activity (129.0 ± 2.8% ) and markedly elevated released CP activity (663.8 ± 4.5% ) relative to psAP-mock (both p < 0.0001) (Fig. 3e-f; Fig. S5f-i; Supplementary Data 4). Conversely, HA-KERP2 overexpression in G3 decreased intracellular CP activity to 87.8 ± 1.1% versus 97.1 ± 1.0% in HA-mock_G3 (p = 0.0031) and reduced released CP activity to 117.1 ± 10.5% versus 155.3 ± 14.1% in HA-mock_G3 (p = 0.0324). We note that CP transcripts change modestly (~2-fold); the enzyme assays serve as an orthogonal functional readout of virulence rather than indicating extensive transcriptional regulation of individual protease genes.

Nuclear Co-immunoprecipitation Reveals KERP2 Involvement in Nucleic-acid Binding and Vesicle-trafficking Networks in E. histolytica
To elucidate KERP2 function through protein-protein interactions, we performed anti-HA co-immunoprecipitation followed by MS on four biological replicates using HM-1:IMSS Cl6 transformants to maximize expression efficiency. HA-KERP2, HA-KERP2∆185−239, and HA-mock lines were fractionated into nuclear (nuclear/organellar-enriched) and cytosolic (cytosolic/light-vesicular) fractions before independent co-IPs. Western blotting confirmed bait recovery, and the HA constructs were identified by MS in inputs and eluates (Fig. S6a-d; Supplementary Data 5a-b). One nuclear HA-mock sample in Trial 3 showed non-specific HA signal and was excluded from analysis a priori. Hit calling required ≥2‑fold higher quantitative value (QV) in HA-KERP2 or HA-KERP2∆185−239 versus the matched HA-mock fraction and detection in ≥2/4 replicates. Under these criteria, the nuclear HA-KERP2 co-IP yielded 75 double-hit and 4 triple-hit interactors, whereas the cytosolic HA-KERP2 co-IP yielded 14 double-hit and 5 triple-hit interactors (Fig. 4a-b, Supplementary Data 5c-d). Gene Ontology enrichment among nuclear interactors included vesicle-related and non-membrane-bound organelle components (including ribosomes), with functional associations in nucleic-acid/protein binding, metabolism, and ribosome biogenesis (Fig. 4c; Fig. S6e-f). In the cytosolic fraction, KEGG enrichment highlighted involvement in ribosome and protein processing in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) (Fig. 4d).
